newsitem.title: USA: Clinton term 2 - In search of a place in history.
newsitem.headline: Clinton term 2 - In search of a place in history.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, the man from a place called Hope, will be in search of a place called history if he wins a second term.

Aides say there is no mystery about his second term agenda. It was all outlined on the campaign trail, and includes balancing the budget, maintaining economic growth, implementing welfare reform and improving education and the environment.

"He achieved a great deal in his first four years," said White House spokesman Mike McCurry, "But there is a strong sense that the most powerful part of his presidency lies in the next four years as we go into a new century."
But beyond Clinton's priorities, which are offshoots of his first term, and a host of small initiatives like encouraging school districts to require student uniforms, there is not much of a road map.

"He hasn't given us a lot of clues," said presidential scholar Stephen Hess of the Brookings Institution. "When a campaign has been about things like school uniforms, it's hard to contend that they have some starry-eyed, exciting new plan that they're about to spring on us."

Would Clinton, who was born in the tiny town of Hope, Arkansas, maintain his 1996 role as a conservative Democrat, or, unfettered by the need to ever run for high office again, would he swing back to the left-leaning Clinton that produced the 1994 health care reform debacle?
"Swinging to the left, I don't think so," said one White House official. "He's got a pretty steady hand right now and he's shown he can work with Republicans and Democrats alike."

Much will depend on the shape of the Congress that Clinton would inherit, whether Republicans will maintain control or whether Democrats will recapture it. But the winning party is likely to have only a slim majority, forcing Clinton to make compromises and form coalitions for his legislative needs.
Experts say this will force the president to make incremental change, not broad, sweeping change.

As outlined in his campaign manifesto book, "Between Hope and History," Clinton wants to place himself in the ranks of so-called "progressive" presidents like Theodore Roosevelt and Woodrow Wilson, who he said "went beyond the conventional thinking of both their parties" to take national action to meet challenges wrought by rapid change.

"Freed from the requirement of running again, a president often and quickly turns to his place in history, not simply what he will be remembered for, but what he wants to be remembered for," said Ken Duberstein, White House chief of staff in Republican President Ronald Reagan's second term.
Clinton, McCurry said, has been reading up on second-term presidencies and found that incumbents ran for re-election based on their record, not on their vision of the future.
Clinton took an alternate course, that "we must build on our record and not sit on it," McCurry said.

"There's never been a re-election campaign by a president that relied so much on specific proposals on what we would do in the next four years," McCurry said, rejecting the idea that Clinton has been vague on his plans.
Budget constraints and the weight of potential scandals could temper the president's aspirations and achievements.
Some analysts say it is the way Clinton goes about balancing the budget that will determine his fate in history.

For instance, it is one thing to promise a balanced budget, yet another to offer the kind of politically unpopular reform it will take to get control of the ballooning spending for Medicare medical insurance for the poor and elderly. Most observers expect whoever wins the presidency to appoint a special bipartisan commission to take on the issue.
"This is the most difficult issue, and it's the issue on which a Clinton legacy may rest," said presidential expert Stephen Wayne, a Georgetown University professor.
Douglas Brinkley, a presidential scholar who is director of the Eisenhower Center at the University of New Orleans, said education reform may hold the key to Clinton's success.

"He wants to be added to that pantheon of progressive reformers," Brinkley said. "Theodore Roosevelt did it by working on the child labor laws. Clinton is trying to do it by building up education. He's now on a path to make the history books as one of the great progressive presidents of the 20th century."
